title: Existence of Limit (LHL = RHL)
notes: **Criterion.** lim(x→a) f(x) = L if and only if LHL = RHL = L with L a finite real number; equality of the two one-sided limits is both necessary and sufficient.
**Worked example — jump.** For f(x) = |x|/x at 0, LHL = −1 and RHL = 1, so lim(x→0) f(x) does not exist even though both one-sided limits do.
**Worked example — hole.** For f(x) = (x² − 9)/(x − 3), both one-sided limits equal 6, so the limit exists at 3 although f(3) is undefined.
**Unbounded behaviour.** If either one-sided limit is ±∞, no finite limit exists; describe the behaviour as an infinite limit instead of a number.
**Piecewise parameters.** To make a piecewise function continuous at a boundary, equate the LHL and RHL expressions and solve for the unknown constant.
**Exam caution.** Oscillating functions such as sin(1/x) near 0 have neither one-sided limit, so no amount of algebraic simplification produces a value.
summary: A two-sided limit exists precisely when the left- and right-hand limits are equal and finite; this criterion is the main test for jumps and piecewise boundaries.
